planting.note: Direct sow in fall on light, sandy, or coastal soils where taller medics struggle; strand medic hugs the ground and tolerates low fertility and brief salt exposure better than most annual medics.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into a firm, weed-free seedbed in early autumn; strand medic's prostrate, mat-forming habit needs open ground to establish without being shaded out by taller companions. It is one of the most salt- and drought-tolerant of the hardseeded annual medics, making it a useful winter cover on light, sandy, or coastal soils where barrel or snail medic underperform. A portion of each seed crop is hard-coated and survives summer dormant in the soil, letting a stand regenerate the following autumn without replanting. Mow or graze before pods fully dry down if limiting volunteer reseeding into a following crop is a priority.
sources: Australian Pastures Genebank species profile: Medicago littoralis

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on neutral to mildly alkaline soils; disc medic grows a taller, more erect stand than most annual medics and fits well into a cereal-legume rotation.

directions: Sow into a firm seedbed once soil has cooled in fall, ideally on neutral to mildly alkaline ground where this species outperforms more acid-tolerant medics. Disc medic grows more upright than barrel or snail medic and forms spineless, flattened, coiled pods that are easier to thresh for seed saving than the spiny pods of related species. As a hardseeded annual it fixes nitrogen through winter and spring, then sets seed and dies back in early summer, leaving a persistent hard-seed bank to regenerate the stand the following season. Grazing or mowing before flowering encourages a denser, leafier stand where biomass rather than seed production is the goal.
sources: Australian Pastures Genebank species profile: Medicago tornata

planting.note: Direct sow in fall; murex medic is notably more tolerant of acid soils than most annual medics, which typically prefer neutral to alkaline conditions.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm autumn seedbed, taking advantage of this species' unusual tolerance for lower soil pH compared with barrel, snail, or disc medic, all of which decline on acid ground. Murex medic forms a low, spreading annual stand that fixes nitrogen over winter and produces distinctive spiny, burr-like pods by late spring. Because it is hardseeded, only part of each season's seed crop germinates the following autumn, giving the stand resilience through dry or poor-establishment years without replanting. Terminate by grazing, mowing, or light cultivation once pods have set to let the stand reseed itself for the next cool season.
sources: Australian Pastures Genebank species profile: Medicago murex

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold-moist stratification, or plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous canopy.

directions: Schreber's aster is among the most shade-tolerant of the native wood asters, thriving in the dry-to-medium duff of closed-canopy deciduous forests where few other asters will flower. It forms broad, heart-shaped basal leaves and spreads gradually by rhizome into loose colonies, sending up airy, branched sprays of small white ray flowers with pale yellow centers from late summer into fall. Plant it under mature hardwoods alongside ferns and other shade natives as a late-season nectar source for small bees and flies when little else is blooming in deep shade. It tolerates root competition and dry shade better than most native asters, making it a good choice for difficult under-tree plantings.
sources: Go Botany (Native Plant Trust) — Eurybia schreberi

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall, or plant divisions in spring, into cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil; this high-elevation native prefers cooler conditions and struggles in hot, humid lowland summers.

directions: Mountain wood-aster is a Southern Appalachian endemic found along high-elevation forest edges, grassy balds, and rocky woodland openings from Virginia to Georgia. It forms a low clump of somewhat leathery, toothed leaves and produces lavender-blue ray flowers with yellow centers from late summer into October, an important late nectar source for native bees and butterflies at elevations above roughly 3,000 feet. Because it is adapted to cool mountain summers, it performs best in partial, dappled shade with consistently moist soil and declines where summer nights stay warm and humid. Site it in a cool woodland garden alongside other high-elevation natives such as Rhododendron and Galax for the most reliable long-term performance.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley's Flora)

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for cold stratification over winter (germination is often erratic and can take a full season), or plant nursery divisions in spring into rich, well-drained woodland soil.

directions: Horse gentian is a coarse-textured, upright native perennial of rich deciduous woodlands and woodland edges across eastern and central North America, named for the large, felty, perfoliate leaves that clasp directly around each stem. In late spring it bears small, dull maroon to greenish-purple tubular flowers tucked in the leaf axils, visited chiefly by bumblebees and other long-tongued native bees, followed in summer by clusters of orange-red, berry-like fruit that persist into fall and feed birds. It is easy to grow in ordinary woodland soil once established and tolerates root competition from trees better than many showier woodland natives. Use it as an understory filler in a naturalistic shade garden, where its unusual flowers and colorful fruit add interest between the spring-ephemeral and fall-aster seasons.

planting.note: Best planted from divisions or container plants in spring or fall into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; variegation is most reliably reproduced by division rather than seed.

directions: Variegated zigzag goldenrod is a foliage-selected form of the woodland native Solidago flexicaulis, its broad, toothed leaves splashed with irregular cream to yellow margins that brighten shaded beds from spring through fall, well before the small, bright-yellow, late-season flower clusters open along the characteristically zigzagging stems. Like the wild species it is among the most shade-adapted of the goldenrods, thriving in the dappled to fairly deep shade of a deciduous woodland understory alongside ferns, Solomon's seal, and hostas. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor, keep the variegation crisp, and prevent overly vigorous plain-green reversion shoots from taking over the clump. Its late-summer and fall bloom offers valuable nectar for woodland-edge pollinators at a time when few other shade perennials are still flowering.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Solidago Trial Garden Report
